headline: Six newborn dolphins offer Cambodia a chance to save sacred river species
meta_description: Cambodia's critically endangered Irrawaddy dolphins receive hope as six calves are born along the Mekong, raising the population to 118.
summary_short: Six newborn Irrawaddy dolphins born this year in Cambodia's Mekong River signal that this critically endangered species can recover with proper protection.
body:
Six newborn calves born this year along a 120-kilometer stretch of Cambodia's Mekong River have brought unexpected hope to conservationists working to save the critically endangered Irrawaddy dolphin. The births have raised the population to an estimated 118 individuals, a modest but meaningful gain for a species regarded as sacred throughout Cambodia and Laos, where they represent the ancestral spirit of the river. For the communities living along the waterway, these dolphins are far more than cultural symbols—they generate vital ecotourism income. Boat driver Heang Koeurn, who guides visitors to the Kampi dolphin pool, a protected 60-meter-deep stretch in Kratie province, explains the economic lifeline simply: "People here can make more income from tourists by driving them to see the beauty of Irrawaddy dolphins."

Yet recovery remains fragile. The population stands far below late-1990s estimates of roughly 200 individuals, devastated by electrofishing, habitat degradation, and gillnet entanglement—particularly lethal for calves. The construction of more than 160 dams across the Mekong Basin has disrupted the river's hydrology and fish populations that dolphins depend on for food. In 2022, the last dolphin in the Anlong Chheu Teal pool died from net entanglement, serving as a stark reminder of the stakes.

Since 2014, Cambodia's Fisheries Administration and WWF-Cambodia have partnered to balance conservation with local fishing needs. River guards earn just $5 to $7.50 daily—meager compensation for facing risks from armed illegal fishers—yet they persist. "The income is small, but it is out of the goodness of our hearts we keep doing this job," said one guard, Kem Sophat. As officials note, the recent births prove recovery is possible if threats are controlled. But the work, they emphasize, is far from finished.
quick_facts: Six calves born in 2024 along 120-km Mekong stretch in Kratie and Stung Treng
Population now estimated at 118 individuals, down from ~200 in late 1990s
Irrawaddy dolphins regarded as sacred, representing ancestral river spirits
River guards earn $5–$7.50 daily protecting dolphins from illegal fishing
Over 160 dams in Mekong Basin disrupt habitat and food sources
